Analog Electronics
Op Amp Slew Rate: Meaning, SR = 2πfVp Formula, Full Power Bandwidth, LM741 vs TL081 Example and Distortion Fixes

Slew rate decides how fast an amplifier output can swing, and a slow part quietly turns clean sine waves into triangles. Below you get the formula, a worked LM741 example, a calculator and a practical way to select a part for real circuits.

SR = 2πfVp Full Power Bandwidth Free Calculator LM741 vs TL081 Troubleshooting

Slew rate is the speed limit of an amplifier output, measured in volts per microsecond. Here is how to calculate the value your signal needs and pick a part that meets it.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn what op amp slew rate means, how to calculate it and how to choose an amplifier that will not distort your signal.
Quick Answer

What is op amp slew rate and how do you calculate it?

Op amp slew rate is the maximum rate of change of the output voltage, given in V/µs. For a sine wave the required value is SR = 2πf × Vpeak, so a 20 kHz signal with 10 V peak needs about 1.26 V/µs. An LM741 rated at 0.5 V/µs cannot do this and will output a distorted triangle, while a TL081 at 13 V/µs handles it easily.

What Is Op Amp Slew Rate?

Op amp slew rate is the fastest speed at which the output voltage of an operational amplifier can rise or fall, normally written in volts per microsecond (V/µs). When the input asks the output to change faster than this limit, the output simply ramps at its maximum speed and the waveform gets distorted.

Key Facts
  • Unit: volts per microsecond (V/µs), quoted as a typical value in the datasheet.
  • Sine wave requirement: SR = 2π × f × Vpeak.
  • Full power bandwidth: FPBW = SR ÷ (2π × Vpeak).
  • LM741 is about 0.5 V/µs and TL081 is about 13 V/µs, as listed in the Texas Instruments datasheets.
  • Slew rate is a large signal limit, while gain bandwidth product is a small signal limit.

If you are new to amplifiers, first revise the basics of the operational amplifier such as open loop gain and the virtual short. Slew rate becomes important the moment your design has a large output swing at a reasonably high frequency, for example a unity gain buffer driving a fast square wave.

Do You Know?

Texas Instruments explains in its note Ramping Up on Slew Rate that some modern CMOS amplifiers use a slew boost circuit. These parts slew much faster for large input steps than for small ones, so the datasheet number depends on the test condition.

Why Does the Slew Rate Limit Happen Inside an Op Amp?

The limit happens because the input stage can only supply a fixed maximum current to charge the internal compensation capacitor. A capacitor charged by a fixed current produces a voltage ramp, and that ramp speed is the slew rate.

Large input stepThe differential input voltage becomes big for a moment.
Input stage saturatesThe input pair delivers its full tail current and no more.
Compensation capacitorCc charges at a constant rate set by that current.
Output rampThe output rises in a straight line until feedback catches up.
SR = Imax ÷ Cc
Imax = maximum input stage current
Cc = internal compensation capacitor

All About Circuits shows the LM124 internal schematic where the compensation capacitor is clearly labelled, and the same idea applies to the classic 741. A small tail current or a big capacitor gives a slow amplifier, so low power parts are usually slow parts.

Quick Tip

Slew rate does not change with closed loop gain in the way bandwidth does. A gain of 1 or a gain of 10 still gives roughly the same V/µs, but higher gain makes the output swing bigger and so the limit is reached sooner.

How to Calculate Required Op Amp Slew Rate?

For a sine wave, multiply 2π by the frequency and by the peak output voltage, then convert the result to V/µs. The steepest point of a sine wave is at the zero crossing, and its slope there equals 2πfVp.

v(t) = Vp sin(2πft)
Max slope = SR = 2π × f × Vp
Full power bandwidth:
FPBW = SR ÷ (2π × Vp)
1
Find peak output
Use the output peak, not the input peak, so multiply input by the stage gain first.
2
Find highest frequency
Take the top frequency the circuit must pass without distortion.
3
Apply SR = 2πfVp
The answer comes in V/s, so divide by one million to get V/µs.
4
Add margin
Choose an amplifier with at least two to five times the calculated value.

For a square or step signal, the rule is different because the edge is the limit. Rise time from 10 % to 90 % is roughly 0.8 × step size ÷ SR when the output is fully slew limited.

Solved Example: Can an LM741 Pass a 20 kHz, 10 V Peak Signal?

No, an LM741 cannot pass this signal cleanly because it needs 1.26 V/µs and the part offers only about 0.5 V/µs. Its full power bandwidth at 10 V peak works out to less than 8 kHz.

Given: f = 20 kHz, Vp = 10 V, LM741 SR = 0.5 V/µs
SR needed = 2 × 3.1416 × 20000 × 10
SR needed = 1,256,637 V/s = 1.26 V/µs
FPBW = 0.5 × 106 ÷ (2 × 3.1416 × 10)
FPBW = 7.96 kHz
Op Amp Slew Rate Calculator
Result
Required SR 1.26 V/µs, FPBW of chosen op amp 7.96 kHz, too slow, expect distortion

Change the last field to 13, the typical figure for a TL081, and the calculator shows a full power bandwidth above 200 kHz. With that one change, the same circuit handles any audio range signal comfortably.

In a non inverting amplifier with a gain of 11 and 1 V peak input, the output peak becomes 11 V. Always do the slew check at the output, and an op amp gain calculator helps you get that output figure quickly.

Slew Rate vs Bandwidth: What Is the Difference?

Slew rate is a large signal speed limit in V/µs, while gain bandwidth product is a small signal frequency limit in MHz. A circuit must satisfy both, and for big outputs the slew limit usually bites first.

PointSlew rate (SR)Gain bandwidth (GBW)
Signal sizeLarge signalSmall signal
UnitV/µsMHz
Depends onOutput amplitudeClosed loop gain
Distortion typeTriangle shaped, nonlinearAmplitude roll off, linear
FormulaFPBW = SR ÷ 2πVpf = GBW ÷ gain
LM741 typical0.5 V/µsAbout 1 MHz

An easy way to remember it: bandwidth asks whether the amplifier can follow small fast wiggles and slew rate asks whether it can make big fast swings. The inverting amplifier gain formula tells you the gain, and from that you can check both limits in two lines.

High slew rate amplifier: advantages
  • Clean large signal output at higher frequency
  • Fast settling for ADC drivers and sample and hold circuits
  • Sharp edges in comparators and pulse circuits
High slew rate amplifier: trade offs
  • Usually higher supply current and power
  • Can be harder to keep stable with capacitive loads
  • Often more noise or offset at the same price

How to Select an Op Amp by Slew Rate?

Calculate the slew rate your worst case signal needs, add a margin of two to five times, and then shortlist parts whose typical datasheet value is above that number. After that, check bandwidth, noise, supply range and output swing.

LM358

General purpose dual amplifier listed by Texas Instruments at about 0.3 V/µs typical.

Best for: Slow sensor signals and DC level shifting
0.3 V/µs
LM741

The classic teaching part with about 0.5 V/µs typical in the TI datasheet.

Best for: Lab practicals and low frequency work
0.5 V/µs
NE5532

Low noise dual amplifier widely used in audio, with about 9 V/µs typical.

Best for: Audio preamps and mixers
9 V/µs
TL081

JFET input amplifier listed at about 13 V/µs typical by Texas Instruments.

Best for: Active filters and audio range signal chains
13 V/µs

For an active Sallen and Key filter at audio frequencies, a TL081 class part is a safe and cheap choice. For a fast ADC driver, look at the settling time figure as well, because slewing plus settling decides when the sample is valid.

  • Use the output peak voltage after gain, not the input peak.
  • Use the highest frequency or the fastest edge in the signal.
  • Compare with the typical and the minimum slew rate in the datasheet.
  • Check rising and falling slew rate separately, as some parts differ.
  • Keep a margin of at least two times for temperature and part spread.
Do You Know?

Many datasheets list slew rate at unity gain with a specific load resistor and capacitor. A heavier capacitive load in your board can make the real output slower than the printed figure.

What Causes Slew Rate Distortion and How to Fix It?

Slew rate distortion happens when the output cannot keep up, so a sine wave turns into a triangle and square wave edges become slow ramps. To fix it, lower the amplitude or frequency, or move to a faster amplifier.

Symptom on scopeLikely causeField fix
Sine becomes triangleSR below 2πfVpUse a faster part or reduce gain
Distortion only at high volumeLarge swing reaches SR limitReduce peak swing or raise SR
Slow square wave edgesFully slewing outputCheck rise time against 0.8 × step ÷ SR
Rising and falling slopes differAsymmetric internal currentsPick a part with symmetric SR
Ringing after the rampCapacitive load or low phase marginAdd an isolation resistor at the output

Slew limited output adds odd harmonics, much like the harmonic distortion and THD you see in power systems. In audio this sound is called transient intermodulation distortion, and it is easy to hear at high volume.

Advertisement

Where Does Slew Rate Matter in Instrumentation?

Slew rate matters wherever an amplifier must make large and fast output swings, such as ADC drivers, comparators, pulse circuits and active filters. In slow process signals like a 4 to 20 mA loop, it is rarely the limiting factor.

ADC driver
Must slew and settle within one conversion period.
Comparator built from op amp
Slow slew gives late and soft switching edges.
Precision rectifier
Output must jump across two diode drops at each zero crossing.
Photodiode front end
Fast light pulses need a quick transimpedance stage.

For example, when you use an op amp as one of the comparator circuits, the output must swing from rail to rail, and a slow part gives very soft edges. The precision rectifier and the transimpedance amplifier for photodiodes are two more circuits where students often meet this limit in the lab.

Myth: Higher gain bandwidth product always means a higher slew rate.
Fact: They are separate specifications, and two parts with the same GBW can have very different V/µs values.
Myth: Slew rate only matters for square waves.
Fact: Sine waves are limited too, and the peak slope 2πfVp sets the need.
Myth: Reducing gain fixes slew distortion every time.
Fact: Lower gain helps only because it lowers the output swing, not because SR itself increases.
Quick Tip

On the bench, feed a square wave and measure the slope of the output edge between 10 % and 90 % on the scope. Divide the voltage change by the time and you have the real slew rate of your board.

Op Amp Slew Rate FAQ

What is the difference between op amp slew rate and bandwidth with example?

Slew rate limits large signal speed in V/µs, while gain bandwidth product limits small signal frequency in MHz.

An LM741 has about 1 MHz GBW, yet at 10 V peak its slew rate of 0.5 V/µs limits clean output to under 8 kHz.

How to calculate the required slew rate of an op amp step by step?

Take the output peak voltage, multiply it by 2π and by the highest frequency, then divide by one million to get V/µs.

For 5 V peak at 50 kHz, the answer is 2 × 3.1416 × 50000 × 5, which gives about 1.57 V/µs.

What happens to a sine wave when the slew rate is too low?

The sine wave turns into a triangle shaped wave because the output can only ramp at its maximum speed.

The peak amplitude also drops, and the output gains odd harmonics that raise distortion, which is clearly visible on an oscilloscope.

Which op amp is best for high slew rate audio and filter circuits?

For audio range work, parts like the TL081 at about 13 V/µs or the NE5532 at about 9 V/µs are common choices.

Always calculate 2πfVp for your own signal first, then pick a part with two to five times that value.

How do you calculate full power bandwidth from the slew rate value?

Divide the slew rate in V/s by 2π times the peak output voltage.

For an amplifier with 13 V/µs at 10 V peak, the full power bandwidth is 13000000 ÷ 62.83, which gives roughly 207 kHz for a clean, undistorted sine output.

What is the common mistake engineers make when checking op amp slew rate?

The most common mistake is using the input peak voltage instead of the output peak after gain.

A gain of 10 multiplies the needed slew rate by 10, so a part that looked fine on paper can distort badly on the bench.

What We Learn Today

  • Op amp slew rate is the maximum output voltage change per microsecond, and it is set by input stage current charging the compensation capacitor.
  • The required value for a sine wave is SR = 2πfVp, and full power bandwidth equals the slew rate divided by 2π times the peak voltage.
  • Choose an amplifier with two to five times the calculated slew rate and always use the output peak after gain in the calculation.
